newsitem.title: GERMANY: German SPD calls for EIB-funded jobs programme.
newsitem.headline: German SPD calls for EIB-funded jobs programme.

text.p: Germany's opposition Social Democrats (SPD) on Monday called for a shift in European policy including a 20-billion-mark jobs programme that would be financed by the European Investment Bank (EIB).

The SPD, facing elections next year and keen to grab the momentum after leftist victories at the polls in Britain and France, said Chancellor Helmut Kohl's centre-right coalition has not delivered on promises of jobs and increased investment.
SPD chairman Oskar Lafontaine said the French and British elections showed that such broken promises would not be tolerated by the broad population.

"The SPD wants more than just a change in government. We want a change in policy towards one that puts employment, economic growth with respect for the environment and social justice back at centre stage," said Lafontaine.

The SPD statement came as EU leaders gathered in Amsterdam for an annual summit meeting side-tracked by the insistence of France's newly-elected Socialist government that jobs and economic growth, rather than just fiscal rectitude, should be put at the heart of EU policy.

The German government has offered to talk about closer coordination of economic and employment policies, but has staunchly rejected any type of jobs scheme that would involve additional financing from EU member states.

Ernst Schwanhold, economic spokesman for the SPD in parliament, told a news conference in Bonn that it was possible to finance a programme for jobs and economic growth without additional spending by member states.

He proposed a programme financed largely through existing EIB funds to carry out the EU's trans-European networks programme to expand telecommunications and railway networks and also to support enterprise start-ups.

Schwanhold said Germany's share of EIB profits alone totalled 400 million marks in 1996, so there would be no need for additional state spending. Such a programme would also attract private sector investment, he said.
Schwanhold sharply criticised Chancellor Helmut Kohl's centre-right government for failing to consider job promotion measures as part of its tax reform.
"It is necessary to bring forward the parts of the tax reform that will affect investment and job creation," Schwanhold said.
"But the coalition only makes decisions that serve to extend the unity of the government. This give no signals to industry," he added. -- William Boston, Bonn Newsroom, 49 228 26097 150
